name: Executive order of June 14, 1867 setting apart the first Coeur d'Alene reserve
promises: The President established a reserve known as the Coeur d'Alene reserve for the Coeur d'Alene and others of northern Idaho, from the head of the Latah to the St. Joseph River at the old mission and west to the Washington line, including about 250,000 acres (Royce schedule).
landTaken: Royce shows the boundaries of this original reserve by a dotted line within the reserve set apart by executive order of November 8, 1873, which took it in.
today: The 1867 reserve was replaced by the larger reservation of November 8, 1873, researched as cession-1873-11-08-coeur-d-al-ne.

sources.title: Charles C. Royce, Indian Land Cessions in the United States (18th Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899), schedule p. 846

Coeur d'Alene Tribe of Indians v. United States, Docket 81, Findings of Fact (4 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1, August 26, 1955)
sources.publisher: Indian Claims Commission Decisions, Oklahoma State University Library

openQuestions: Not a treaty: an executive order reserve, enlarged in 1873. No court, Commission or Act finding about the 1867 reserve itself was found; the Docket 81 findings speak of the 1873 agreement and reservation, not this order.

treaties.json maps this record to Royce area 552, the Coeur d'Alene country outside the 1873 reservation. The Indian Claims Commission (Docket 81) found the consideration for those outside lands, with title passing March 3, 1891, unconscionable; that finding belongs to the 1891 records, not to this order.
The order text was read through Royce only; the University of Georgia copy (552r.pdf) did not load.
